title: Introducing "Behind The Memo": Selling Out
summary:
There are very few opportunities to time the markets
when the market is at such an extreme of over or undervaluation that the evidence is compelling and the
probability of being right is high. Managing a portfolio of investments requires consistent re-evaluation of the value
proposition. So being in the market, enjoying that compound growth, staying with the process, I believe
really is the most important thing.

positions.commentary: The speaker cites Amazon as an example of a stock that has risen hugely over 20 years, noting that holding such a winner makes sense despite the psychological urge to sell.

thesis: This episode uses Amazon as a specific example to argue that holding a massive long-term winner is the right investment decision, even when the psychological urge to sell arises. The core argument is that the performance of such a stock over two decades validates the strategy of staying invested despite the temptation to exit.

claims.claim: The speaker cites Amazon as an example of a stock that has risen hugely over 20 years, noting that holding such a winner makes sense despite the psychological urge to sell.
claims.quote: An example of that, which I refer to in the memo, is Amazon. And in the last 20 years, and in the last 20 years, and you would have to have talked yourself out of selling.

numbers.quote: Let's say that rather than 10 and a half, the stock market is going to compound at 7% in the future.

numbers.quote: If you can invest at 10.5% and merely hold it, a dollar invested today will grow to $147 in 50 years.

numbers.quote: That dollar is still going to compound to $29 in 50 years.
